# Steve Eisman Answers YOUR Investing Questions | The Real Eisman Playbook Episode 23

First listed: 2025-09-01 | Evaluation cutoff: 2026-11-10

[Back to library](../README.md)

## Source versions

- [YouTube: Steve Eisman Answers YOUR Investing Questions | The Real Eisman Playbook Episode 23](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VzEOuW--Hds) - 2025-09-01
- [Substack: Steve Eisman Answers YOUR Investing Questions | The Real Eisman Playbook Episode 23](https://realeismanplaybook.substack.com/p/steve-eisman-answers-your-investing-c2f) - 2025-09-01

Earliest listed publication among matched versions, not proof of an unedited contemporaneous archive. Claim timestamps refer to the reviewed version.

## Summary

Eisman explains a story-driven investing process grounded in independent data, pricing power, balance sheets and long holding periods. He favors US index exposure and AI, rejects stock compensation as economically free, and revisits MLP financing failures. The housing lock-in mechanism and several accounting principles are sound, but mortgage arithmetic exaggerates the required price decline. His account of deposit rates and the Fed constitutional origin is wrong, and EU trade authority is oversimplified. These explanatory errors are separated from untested long-term portfolio preferences and personal disclosures.

Entire transcript read. Useful company-level accounting and risk principles coexist with weaker monetary/legal explanations. Strong long-term US enthusiasm has no precise return target. The viewer recovery context runs five years, so no premature performance grade is assigned. Unverified anecdotes and portfolio disclosures remain unverified, not adverse grades.

### 035. Moving from a 3% to 4% mortgage to about 6.5% would require roughly halving the house price to keep the same monthly payment.

For equal 30-year fully amortizing terms, proportional down payments and principal-and-interest-only payments, payment factor f(r)=r/[1-(1+r)^(-360)], with monthly r. ## Framework and tools

- Require a company story beyond cheap valuation.
- Cross-check management narratives with independent operating data.
- Analyze cash retention, leverage and security rights together.
- Treat stock compensation as an economic transfer.
- Recognize personal timing and lifestyle constraints in portfolio design.
- Watch for unsupported macro certainty and arithmetic shortcuts.

Tools and charts discussed, not a complete visual inspection:

- Quarterly earnings calls and management language
- Industry periodicals and securitization databases
- Credit-rating and payment-network concentration
- S&P 500 and Nasdaq-100 index funds
- Mortgage payment comparisons
- MLP distribution coverage, leverage and incentive distribution rights
- GAAP versus adjusted EPS and stock compensation
- Federal funds rate and yield-curve distinctions

## Source cautions

Steve Eisman is the sole substantive speaker; viewer questions are distinguished from his responses.
- Opening montage duplicates later answers.
- Viewer questions are quoted and are not Eisman assertions; their hypothetical trades and claims are excluded unless he endorses them.
- He corrects Tarullo formal title but incorrectly mentions Chair Powell in the historical explanation; Tarullo left under Yellen.
- The broad technology-weight estimate uses an informal sector definition.
- Mortgage comparison assumes equal loan terms and proportional down payments for the arithmetic test.
- MLP index identity and total-return treatment are unspecified.
